# J1 Data Preparation (Joint)

# J1.1 Download

Adjusted prices are revised by Yahoo whenever dividends and splits are reprocessed, so the raw downloads are
saved once to `data_snapshot.rds` and reused on every later run. This keeps every number in the appendix and
the report identical. Deleting the file forces a fresh download.

```{r j1-download}
tickers    <- c("AWR", "BBY", "CMCSA", "COP", "ELA", "KR", "MCD", "MSFT", "NEU", "SLB")
start_date <- as.Date("2014-12-01")
end_date   <- as.Date("2026-09-01")
snapshot   <- "data_snapshot.rds"

if (file.exists(snapshot)) {
  snap          <- readRDS(snapshot)
  daily_list    <- snap$daily_list
  ff_raw        <- snap$ff_raw
  download_date <- snap$download_date
} else {
  get_adjusted <- function(tk) {
    x <- tryCatch(getSymbols(tk, src = "yahoo", from = start_date, to = end_date,
                             auto.assign = FALSE),
                  error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(x)) NULL else Ad(x)
  }
  daily_list <- setNames(lapply(tickers, get_adjusted), tickers)

  failed <- tickers[sapply(daily_list, is.null)]
  if (length(failed) > 0) stop("Download failed for: ", paste(failed, collapse = ", "))

  ff_raw <- tryCatch(getSymbols("FEDFUNDS", src = "FRED", auto.assign = FALSE),
                     error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(ff_raw)) {
    # Fallback: CSV saved manually from https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/FEDFUNDS
    ff_csv <- read.csv("FEDFUNDS.csv")
    ff_raw <- xts(ff_csv[[2]], order.by = as.Date(ff_csv[[1]]))
  }

  download_date <- Sys.Date()
  saveRDS(list(daily_list = daily_list, ff_raw = ff_raw, download_date = download_date), snapshot)
}

cat("Data downloaded on:", format(download_date), "\n")
```

# J1.2 Download audit

```{r j1-audit}
data_log <- data.frame(
  Ticker         = tickers,
  First_date     = as.Date(sapply(daily_list, function(x) as.character(start(x)))),
  Last_date      = as.Date(sapply(daily_list, function(x) as.character(end(x)))),
  Daily_obs      = sapply(daily_list, nrow),
  Missing_prices = sapply(daily_list, function(x) sum(is.na(x))),
  row.names = NULL
)
kable(data_log, caption = "Table J1.1: Daily adjusted-price download audit")
```

All ten series were downloaded successfully from Yahoo Finance as adjusted closing prices, which account for
dividends and stock splits. Each series covers 1 December 2014 to 31 August 2026 (2,954 trading days) with no
missing observations, so the series are aligned on identical trading dates. Yahoo treats the end date
(1 September 2026) as exclusive, so no September 2026 data were returned. Two tickers were checked for
corporate changes: Envela (ELA, formerly DGSE Companies) and SLB (formerly Schlumberger, ticker unchanged).
Yahoo provides continuous adjusted histories for both, so no manual adjustment was required.

# J1.3 Monthly prices and incomplete months

Monthly observations are the last adjusted price of each calendar month. The December 2014 month-end price is
the base for the January 2015 return. Any September 2026 observation would be an incomplete month and is
removed, so August 2026 is the final completed month. The filter is kept as a safeguard even though Table J1.1
shows that no September data were downloaded.

```{r j1-monthly}
month_end <- function(x) {
  m <- x[endpoints(x, on = "months")]
  index(m) <- as.yearmon(index(m))
  m
}

prices_m <- do.call(merge, lapply(daily_list, month_end))
colnames(prices_m) <- tickers

last_full_month <- as.yearmon("2026-08")
prices_m <- prices_m[index(prices_m) <= last_full_month]

stopifnot(start(prices_m) == as.yearmon("2014-12"))
colSums(is.na(prices_m))
```

# J1.4 Arithmetic monthly returns

$r_{i,t} = (P_{i,t} - P_{i,t-1}) / P_{i,t-1}$

```{r j1-returns}
returns_m <- prices_m / lag.xts(prices_m, k = 1) - 1
returns_m <- returns_m[-1, ]

colSums(is.na(returns_m))

zero_idx <- which(coredata(returns_m) == 0, arr.ind = TRUE)
kable(data.frame(Month  = format(index(returns_m)[zero_idx[, "row"]]),
                 Ticker = colnames(returns_m)[zero_idx[, "col"]]),
      caption = "Table J1.2: Months with an exactly zero return")
```

```{r j1-slb-check}
# SLB's zero-return month (July 2025) checked against daily prices
daily_list$SLB["2025-06-25/2025-07-03"]
daily_list$SLB["2025-07-25/2025-08-05"]
```

Five monthly returns are exactly zero. The four ELA cases (Aug 2016, Jan 2017, Jul 2018, Dec 2021) are
consistent with infrequent trading in this small-cap stock, where the month-end price repeats the last traded
price. The SLB case (Jul 2025, validation sample) was checked against daily prices: trading was normal on the
surrounding days, and the stock closed at an identical price on 30 June and 31 July 2025, with no dividend in
between. All five observations are therefore genuine and were retained, because deleting real observations
would bias return and volatility estimates.

# J1.5 Risk-free rate

FEDFUNDS is the monthly average of the daily effective Federal Funds Rate, quoted in percent per annum. It is
converted to a monthly decimal return by geometric de-annualisation:

$r_{f,t} = (1 + FF_t/100)^{1/12} - 1$

The rate for month *t* (the average over month *t*) is matched to the stock return earned over month *t*.

```{r j1-riskfree}
ff <- ff_raw
index(ff) <- as.yearmon(index(ff))
ff <- ff[index(ff) >= as.yearmon("2015-01") & index(ff) <= last_full_month]

rf_m <- (1 + ff / 100)^(1 / 12) - 1
colnames(rf_m) <- "RF"

rows <- c(1, 60, 120, nrow(ff))
kable(data.frame(Month            = format(index(ff))[rows],
                 FF_annual_pct    = round(as.numeric(ff)[rows], 2),
                 RF_geometric_pct = round(100 * as.numeric(rf_m)[rows], 4),
                 RF_simple_pct    = round(as.numeric(ff)[rows] / 12, 4)),
      caption = "Table J1.3: Federal Funds Rate conversion examples (monthly %)")
```

The geometric conversion compounds back to the quoted annual rate over twelve months and puts the risk-free
return in the same units as the monthly stock returns. The simple method (FF/12) gives almost identical values,
with a maximum difference of about 0.007 percentage points per month, so the choice has no material effect on
risk-adjusted performance. The risk-free rate ranged from near zero in 2015 to about 0.37% per month in late
2024.

```{r j1-split}
est <- data_all[index(data_all) <= as.yearmon("2024-12")]

stopifnot(nrow(est) == 120, !anyNA(data_all))

R_val <- val[, tickers]; rf_val <- val[, "RF"]
```

The estimation sample (January 2015 – December 2024, 120 months) is used for all estimation and portfolio
construction. The validation sample (January 2025 – August 2026, 20 months) is held back and used only in J3
to evaluate portfolios whose weights have already been frozen.

# J1.7 Shared objects and functions

These objects and helper functions are used by every later section. All are built from the estimation sample;
the validation matrices are created here but not used until J3.

```{r j1-shared}
Rm     <- coredata(R_est)
Rv     <- coredata(R_val)
rf_vec <- as.numeric(rf_est)
rfv    <- as.numeric(rf_val)
k      <- length(tickers)
mu     <- colMeans(Rm)
Sigma  <- cov(Rm)

# Long-only portfolio optimiser (quadratic programming)
#   lambda = NULL, target = NULL : minimum variance
#   lambda = value               : maximise w'mu - (lambda/2) w'Sigma w
#   target = value               : minimum variance for a given expected return
optimise <- function(Sigma, mu = NULL, lambda = NULL, target = NULL, cap = 1) {
  k    <- ncol(Sigma)
  Amat <- matrix(1, k, 1); bvec <- 1; meq <- 1
  if (!is.null(target)) { Amat <- cbind(Amat, mu); bvec <- c(bvec, target); meq <- 2 }
  Amat <- cbind(Amat, diag(k)); bvec <- c(bvec, rep(0, k))
  if (cap < 1) { Amat <- cbind(Amat, -diag(k)); bvec <- c(bvec, rep(-cap, k)) }
  if (is.null(lambda)) { D <- 2 * Sigma; dv <- rep(0, k) } else { D <- lambda * Sigma; dv <- mu }
  w <- solve.QP(D, dv, Amat, bvec, meq = meq)$solution
  w[abs(w) < 1e-8] <- 0
  setNames(w / sum(w), colnames(Sigma))
}

# Performance of fixed weights, rebalanced monthly
port_stats <- function(w, R, rf) {
  rp     <- as.numeric(R %*% w)
  ex     <- rp - rf
  wealth <- cumprod(1 + rp)
  c(Mean_pct        = 100 * mean(rp),
    SD_pct          = 100 * sd(rp),
    Sharpe          = mean(ex) / sd(ex),
    Ann_Mean_pct    = 1200 * mean(rp),
    Ann_SD_pct      = 100 * sqrt(12) * sd(rp),
    Ann_Sharpe      = sqrt(12) * mean(ex) / sd(ex),
    Cumulative_pct  = 100 * (prod(1 + rp) - 1),
    Worst_month_pct = 100 * min(rp),
    Max_DD_pct      = 100 * min(wealth / cummax(wealth) - 1),
    HHI             = sum(w^2),
    Effective_N     = 1 / sum(w^2))
}
stats_table <- function(ports, R, rf) t(sapply(ports, port_stats, R = R, rf = rf))

port_cols <- c("Mean_pct", "SD_pct", "Sharpe", "Ann_Mean_pct", "Ann_SD_pct", "Ann_Sharpe",
               "Worst_month_pct", "Max_DD_pct", "HHI", "Effective_N")
port_digits <- c(2, 2, 3, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 3, 1)

# Formatting helpers for numbers quoted in the text
fmt <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(as.numeric(x), format = "f", digits = d)
fp  <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3)
lst <- function(x) if (length(x) == 0) "none" else paste(x, collapse = ", ")
```

# A1 Return and Volatility Analysis

```{r a1-measures}
ex_est   <- Rm - rf_vec
mean_m   <- colMeans(Rm)
```

# A1 Interpretation

**What the measures capture.** All measures use the estimation sample only (Jan 2015 – Dec 2024), because the
validation sample may not be used for stock screening. The average (arithmetic mean) monthly return measures
the typical one-month gain an investor earned. Volatility (the standard deviation of monthly returns)
measures how widely returns spread around that average, that is, how bumpy and unpredictable the ride is. The
Sharpe ratio divides the average return in excess of the Federal Funds Rate by the volatility of that excess
return. It measures reward per unit of risk, so stocks with very different risk levels can be compared fairly.
Two further measures matter for retirees. The geometric mean is the growth rate actually achieved through
compounding. The maximum drawdown is the largest fall from a previous peak, which is the closest measure to
John's fear of "significant losses".

**Attractive and unattractive stocks.** MSFT is the most attractive stock on almost every measure: the highest
Sharpe ratio (0.32 monthly, 1.11 annualised), the highest compound growth (1.98% per month) and only moderate
volatility (6.3%). MCD is the most defensive stock. It has the lowest volatility (4.9%), the smallest maximum
drawdown (−23.2%) and the second-highest Sharpe ratio (0.23). Over the decade, MCD turned \$1 into \$3.99, the
third-best result of all ten stocks (behind only MSFT and ELA), while carrying the lowest volatility. AWR, a
regulated water utility, also combines low volatility (5.6%) with a modest drawdown. At the other end, SLB is
clearly unattractive: high volatility (11.9%), the worst drawdown (−83.0%) and a Sharpe ratio close to zero.
Its negative geometric mean (−0.44%) means \$1 invested in 2015 was worth only \$0.59 by December 2024
(Table A1.4), despite a positive arithmetic average. COP shows a similar but milder pattern. NEU and CMCSA have
low to moderate risk but deliver little return, so their Sharpe ratios are low.

**Is higher return associated with higher risk?** Across all ten stocks, the correlation between volatility and
average return is positive and significant at the 5% level (r = 0.67, p = 0.036). However, Figure A1.1 shows
this result is driven by a single extreme observation, ELA. With ELA excluded, the correlation becomes negative
and insignificant (r = −0.25, p = 0.51; 95% CI −0.78 to 0.50). For the remaining nine stocks, extra volatility
was therefore not rewarded with extra return over this period. This is consistent with finance theory:
investors are compensated for *systematic* (market-wide) risk, not for total volatility. Much of SLB's and
COP's volatility came from oil-sector shocks (for example, −50.2% and −36.4% in March 2020), and much of ELA's
came from company-specific jumps. Both are largely diversifiable, so neither should be expected to earn a
reward. With only ten stocks and one decade of data, the relationship is also estimated very imprecisely, as
the wide confidence intervals show.

**Relevance to John and Mary.** John's capital-preservation goal favours low volatility, mild worst months and
small drawdowns, which points to MCD, AWR, MSFT and NEU. ELA, SLB and COP are unsuitable for him: each lost
more than 60% from peak to trough at some point. Mary's growth goal favours higher average and compound returns,
which points to MSFT and, to a lesser extent, BBY and MCD. MSFT is notable because it appeals to both: it
delivered the strongest growth without exceptional risk. This suggests the couple's preferences may conflict
less than expected for this stock set.

**Why the highest-return stock is not automatically the best.** ELA has by far the highest arithmetic mean
(3.62% per month), but it is not the best investment, for four reasons.

1. *Volatility drag:* with 20.9% monthly volatility, large losses compound badly. Its geometric mean (1.49%) is
   below MSFT's (1.98%), so \$1 grew to \$5.89 in ELA but to \$10.57 in MSFT (Table A1.4).
2. *Fragility:* the average is driven by a handful of extreme months (+80.6% in June 2019, +69.9% in June 2020,
   −69.2% in May 2015), so it is a very unreliable guide to future returns (see the wide confidence interval
   in A2).
3. *Downside:* an −82.1% drawdown would be devastating for retirees drawing income, who may be forced to sell
   at the bottom.
4. *Portfolio perspective:* the value of a stock depends not on its stand-alone return but on how it combines
   with the others through covariances. That is examined in B1 and A3.

# A2 Expected Returns, Interval Estimation and Normality

```{r a2-intervals}
n      <- nrow(Rm)
t_crit <- qt(0.975, df = n - 1)
se_m   <- sd_m / sqrt(n)

a2_ci <- data.frame(Ticker        = tickers,
                    Mean_pct      = 100 * mean_m,
                    Variance_pct2 = 10000 * sd_m^2,
                    SD_pct        = 100 * sd_m,
                    SE_pct        = 100 * se_m,
                    CI_lower_pct  = 100 * (mean_m - t_crit * se_m),
                    CI_upper_pct  = 100 * (mean_m + t_crit * se_m),
                    CI_width_pct  = 100 * 2 * t_crit * se_m)
a2_ci$Excludes_zero <- ifelse(a2_ci$CI_lower_pct > 0, "Yes", "No")

kable(a2_ci, digits = c(0, 2, 2, 2, 3, 2, 2, 2, 0), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = paste0("Table A2.1: Expected monthly returns with 95% confidence intervals (n = ", n,
                       ", t critical = ", round(t_crit, 3), ")"))

# Cross-check one interval against R's built-in t-test
t.test(Rm[, "MSFT"])$conf.int * 100
```

```{r a2-ciplot, fig.cap = "Figure A2.1: 95% confidence intervals"}
ggplot(a2_ci, aes(x = reorder(Ticker, Mean_pct), y = Mean_pct)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = CI_lower_pct, ymax = CI_upper_pct), width = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 3, colour = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Expected monthly return (%), point estimate and 95% CI") +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r a2-normality}
sw <- lapply(tickers, function(tk) shapiro.test(Rm[, tk]))
jb <- lapply(tickers, function(tk) jarque.bera.test(Rm[, tk]))

norm_tab <- data.frame(Ticker          = tickers,
                       Skewness        = apply(Rm, 2, moments::skewness),
                       Excess_kurtosis = apply(Rm, 2, moments::kurtosis) - 3,
                       SW_W            = sapply(sw, function(t) t$statistic),
                       SW_p            = sapply(sw, function(t) t$p.value),
                       JB_stat         = sapply(jb, function(t) t$statistic),
                       JB_p            = sapply(jb, function(t) t$p.value),
                       row.names = NULL)
norm_tab$Normality_5pct <- ifelse(norm_tab$SW_p > 0.05 & norm_tab$JB_p > 0.05, "Not rejected", "Rejected")
norm_tab$SW_p <- ifelse(norm_tab$SW_p < 0.0001, "<0.0001", sprintf("%.4f", norm_tab$SW_p))
norm_tab$JB_p <- ifelse(norm_tab$JB_p < 0.0001, "<0.0001", sprintf("%.4f", norm_tab$JB_p))

kable(norm_tab, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table A2.2: Skewness, excess kurtosis, Shapiro-Wilk and Jarque-Bera tests (estimation sample)")
```

```{r a2-bootstrap}
set.seed(5002)
boot_ci <- t(apply(Rm, 2, function(r) {
  boot_means <- replicate(5000, mean(sample(r, replace = TRUE)))
  100 * quantile(boot_means, c(0.025, 0.975))
}))

kable(data.frame(Ticker     = tickers,
                 t_lower    = a2_ci$CI_lower_pct, t_upper    = a2_ci$CI_upper_pct,
                 boot_lower = boot_ci[, 1],       boot_upper = boot_ci[, 2]),
      digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table A2.3: t-based vs bootstrap 95% CIs for expected monthly return (%)")
```

# A2 Interpretation

**Meaning of a confidence interval for expected return.** The expected return μ is the true long-run average
monthly return of a stock, which can never be observed directly; the sample mean from 120 months is only an
estimate of it. A 95% confidence interval gives the range of plausible values for μ given the data. Strictly,
it means that if the sampling and interval procedure were repeated many times, about 95% of the intervals
produced would contain the true μ. It does not mean there is a 95% probability that μ lies in this particular
interval. Only MSFT (1.04% to 3.32%) and MCD (0.39% to 2.17%) have intervals entirely above zero (Table A2.1).
For the other eight stocks, including ELA with the highest sample mean, we cannot be 95% confident that the true
expected return is even positive. The heavy overlap of the intervals in Figure A2.1 also suggests that
differences in average returns may not be statistically meaningful; this is tested formally in B2.

**Why interval widths differ, and the role of volatility.** The half-width of each interval is t × s/√n. All
stocks share the same n = 120 and t = 1.980, so width is driven entirely by volatility: each interval is about
0.36 × its standard deviation wide. MCD, the least volatile stock, has the narrowest interval (1.78 percentage
points), while ELA has the widest (7.55 points). Because the standard error shrinks only with √n, halving the
width of an interval would require four times as much data (about 40 years). For highly volatile stocks, even
a decade of history therefore says little about the true expected return.

**Statistical versus economic uncertainty.** Two kinds of uncertainty must be distinguished. *Statistical
uncertainty* concerns how precisely we know μ. Even for MSFT, the interval ranges from roughly 12% to 40% per
year (×12), an economically enormous range for planning a retirement. Economic uncertainty is the
month-to-month variability an investor actually experiences, measured by the standard deviation. For MCD, the
most precisely estimated stock, a typical month could still range from about −8.6% to +11.2% (mean ± 2 SD).
The first affects how much we can trust the optimiser's inputs; the second affects how bumpy the ride feels for
John and Mary.

**Skewness, heavy tails and extreme observations.** Skewness is mild for every stock except ELA (0.78), whose
distribution is stretched to the right by very large positive months such as +80.6% in June 2019
(Table A1.3). The more important departure from normality is heavy tails. COP, ELA and SLB have excess kurtosis
between 2.5 and 3.9, compared with 0 for a normal distribution. This means extreme months, such as SLB's
−50.2% in March 2020, occur far more often than a normal distribution predicts.

**Do the formal tests and the graphs agree?** Largely, yes. Both Shapiro–Wilk and Jarque–Bera reject normality
for COP, ELA and SLB (p < 0.001), and their Q-Q plots (Figure A2.2) show the matching pattern: points follow
the line in the middle but peel away at both ends, with isolated extreme losses at the bottom-left. MCD is the
one case where the tests disagree: Jarque–Bera rejects (p = 0.027) but Shapiro–Wilk does not (p = 0.129). The
Q-Q plot explains why. MCD's distribution is close to normal apart from one or two extreme months at each end;
Jarque–Bera focuses specifically on skewness and kurtosis, which are sensitive to such points, whereas
Shapiro–Wilk assesses overall shape. For BBY, CMCSA, KR, MSFT and NEU, neither test rejects and the Q-Q points
lie close to the line. Because each panel uses its own vertical scale, the plots should be compared by shape
rather than height. Two cautions apply. First, failing to reject normality does not prove it, because with
n = 120 the tests have limited power to detect moderate departures. Second, with ten tests at the 5% level,
roughly one false rejection would be expected by chance alone, although COP, ELA and SLB would remain
significant under any reasonable multiple-testing correction.

**Implications for interval estimation.** The t-interval formally assumes normal returns. However, it concerns
the sample mean, and by the Central Limit Theorem the mean of 120 observations is approximately normal even
when individual returns are not. A bootstrap check, which makes no normality assumption, confirms this: for
nine stocks the bootstrap intervals differ from the t-intervals by at most 0.05 percentage points
(Table A2.3). The exception is ELA, where the right skew shifts the bootstrap interval upward (0.01% to 7.48%)
so that its lower bound only just clears zero. Whether ELA's expected return is "significantly positive"
therefore depends on the method chosen, which is a clear warning that its high average is not a reliable
estimate. Both methods also assume returns are independent from month to month, which may not hold if
volatility clusters in crisis periods.

**Implications for portfolio optimisation.** Mean-variance optimisation describes each stock using only its
expected return, variance and covariances. This is a complete description only if returns are approximately
normal. With heavy tails, variance understates the probability of severe losses, so a portfolio that looks
"low risk" in variance terms may still be exposed to crashes. Correlations also tend to rise in crises: COP and
SLB both had their worst month in March 2020, so diversification can weaken exactly when it is most needed.
Most importantly, the wide confidence intervals show that expected returns are estimated very imprecisely. An
optimiser treats these noisy estimates as exact and tends to pile weight into stocks whose means happen to be
overestimated, a problem often called "error maximisation". This is a key reason for basing John's
capital-preservation portfolio in A3 on minimising variance, which does not rely on expected-return estimates
at all, and for using weight limits to prevent extreme allocations.

# A3 John's Optimal Portfolio

**Objective and constraints.** John's priority is to avoid large fluctuations and significant losses, so his
portfolio minimises portfolio variance:

$$\min_{w} \; \sigma_p^2 = w^\top \Sigma w$$

subject to:

* $\sum_{i=1}^{10} w_i = 1$ (fully invested);
* $w_i \ge 0$ for all $i$ (no short selling, which is unsuitable for retirees);
* in the capped version, $w_i \le 0.30$ (no single company above 30%).

$\Sigma$ is the 10 × 10 covariance matrix estimated from the estimation sample (Jan 2015 – Dec 2024). Expected
returns are deliberately not used in the objective: A2 showed that they are estimated very imprecisely,
whereas variances and covariances are estimated far more reliably.

```{r a3-weights}
w_gmv <- optimise(Sigma)
w_cap <- optimise(Sigma, cap = 0.30)
w_eq  <- setNames(rep(1 / k, k), tickers)
w_mcd <- setNames(as.numeric(tickers == "MCD"), tickers)

stopifnot(abs(sum(w_gmv) - 1) < 1e-8, all(w_gmv >= 0), all(w_cap <= 0.30 + 1e-8))

kable(data.frame(Ticker            = tickers,
                 Min_variance_pct  = 100 * w_gmv,
                 Min_var_30cap_pct = 100 * w_cap,
                 Equal_weight_pct  = 100 * w_eq),
      digits = 1, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Table A3.1: John's portfolio weights (%)")

a3_stats <- stats_table(list("Min variance"           = w_gmv,
                             "Min variance (30% cap)" = w_cap,
                             "Equal weight"           = w_eq,
                             "MCD only"               = w_mcd), Rm, rf_vec)
kable(a3_stats[, port_cols], digits = port_digits,
      caption = "Table A3.2: In-sample performance of John's portfolios vs benchmarks (estimation sample)")
```

```{r a3-risk}
risk_decomp <- function(w, Sigma) {
  cov_p <- as.numeric(Sigma %*% w)
  var_p <- as.numeric(t(w) %*% Sigma %*% w)
  data.frame(Ticker           = names(w),
             Weight_pct       = 100 * w,
             Cov_with_port    = 10000 * cov_p,
             Beta_to_port     = cov_p / var_p,
             Risk_contrib_pct = 100 * w * cov_p / var_p)
}
kable(risk_decomp(w_gmv, Sigma), digits = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 1), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table A3.3: Risk decomposition, minimum-variance portfolio (covariance in %^2)")
kable(risk_decomp(w_cap, Sigma), digits = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 1), row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table A3.4: Risk decomposition, minimum-variance portfolio with 30% cap (covariance in %^2)")
```

```{r a3-weights-plot, fig.cap = "Figure A3.1: John's portfolio weights"}
a3_long <- data.frame(Ticker    = rep(tickers, 2),
                      Portfolio = rep(c("Minimum variance", "Minimum variance, 30% cap"), each = k),
                      Weight    = 100 * c(w_gmv, w_cap))

ggplot(a3_long, aes(Ticker, Weight, fill = Portfolio)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Portfolio weight (%)", fill = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r a3-check, fig.cap = "Figure A3.2: John's portfolios among random portfolios"}
# Independent check: no random long-only portfolio should have lower volatility
set.seed(5002)
W       <- matrix(rexp(20000 * k), ncol = k)
W       <- W / rowSums(W)
rand_sd <- sqrt(rowSums((W %*% Sigma) * W))

c(lowest_random_SD_pct = 100 * min(rand_sd),
  optimiser_SD_pct     = 100 * sqrt(as.numeric(t(w_gmv) %*% Sigma %*% w_gmv)))

cloud      <- data.frame(SD = 100 * rand_sd, Mean = 100 * as.numeric(W %*% mu))
stocks_pts <- data.frame(Label = tickers, SD = 100 * sd_m, Mean = 100 * mean_m)
port_pts   <- data.frame(Label = rownames(a3_stats),
                         SD = a3_stats[, "SD_pct"], Mean = a3_stats[, "Mean_pct"])

ggplot() +
  geom_point(data = cloud, aes(SD, Mean), colour = "grey80", size = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(data = stocks_pts, aes(SD, Mean), colour = "grey30") +
  geom_text(data = stocks_pts, aes(SD, Mean, label = Label), vjust = -0.8, size = 3) +
  geom_point(data = port_pts, aes(SD, Mean, colour = Label), size = 3.5) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(3, 13), ylim = c(0, 2.6)) +
  labs(x = "Volatility (monthly SD, %)", y = "Expected monthly return (%)", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Grey cloud: random long-only portfolios. The two minimum-variance points coincide (cap not binding).\nELA (SD 20.9%) lies off the chart.") +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

# A3 Interpretation

**Result and choice between the two versions.** The minimum-variance portfolio invests in seven of the ten
stocks: MCD 25.0%, NEU 24.0%, AWR 21.4%, MSFT 13.8%, KR 9.0%, COP 5.1% and ELA 1.7%, with nothing in BBY, CMCSA or
SLB (Table A3.1, Figure A3.1). The 30% cap does not bind, because the largest unconstrained weight is 25%, so the
capped and uncapped solutions are identical (Tables A3.1 to A3.4). The cap is still reported because it is a
sensible policy safeguard for a retiree; the fact that it is not needed shows that the optimiser has produced a
naturally spread-out portfolio rather than a concentrated bet. This portfolio is John's optimal allocation. On the
estimation sample it has an expected return of 1.15% per month (13.8% a year), volatility of 3.54% per month
(12.3% a year) and a Sharpe ratio of 0.284 per month (0.99 annualised) (Table A3.2). As an independent check,
none of 20,000 randomly generated long-only portfolios had lower volatility: the lowest was
`r round(100 * min(rand_sd), 2)`%, compared with the optimiser's
`r round(100 * sqrt(as.numeric(t(w_gmv) %*% Sigma %*% w_gmv)), 2)`%, and Figure A3.2 shows the portfolio on the
left edge of every achievable combination.

**Why this objective represents capital preservation.** John wants to avoid large fluctuations and significant
losses. Portfolio variance measures exactly the size of fluctuations around the average, and smaller fluctuations
also mean smaller losses in bad months: the portfolio's worst month was −8.5% and its largest peak-to-trough fall
−12.3%, compared with −14.8% and −23.2% for MCD, the safest single stock (Table A3.2). The objective deliberately
ignores expected returns. A2 showed that expected returns are estimated so imprecisely that only two stocks are
statistically positive; an objective that chased them would be driven largely by estimation error, which is the
opposite of what a cautious investor wants.

**Why the optimiser assigns these weights.** At the minimum-variance solution, every stock that is held must
contribute to portfolio risk at exactly the same rate. Formally, its covariance with the portfolio, (Σw)ᵢ, equals
the portfolio variance σp², so its "beta to the portfolio" is exactly 1. If one held stock added more risk at the
margin than another, moving a little money from the first to the second would lower total risk, so the portfolio
could not yet be at its minimum. Table A3.3 confirms this: all seven held stocks have a covariance with the
portfolio of 12.54 (%)², which equals the portfolio variance (3.54² ≈ 12.54), and a beta of 1.000. A direct
consequence is that, in this portfolio, each stock's share of total risk equals its weight.

**How expected returns, variances and covariances shape the solution.** Expected returns play no role in John's
objective; only variances and covariances do. Low variance earns a large weight, which is why MCD (the lowest
volatility, 4.9%), AWR (5.6%) and NEU (5.7%) together make up about 70% of the portfolio. NEU's place is notable:
it has one of the lowest average returns (0.54% a month), but the optimiser does not reward return, only the
ability to calm the portfolio. Covariance matters as much as variance. ELA is the most volatile stock (20.9% a
month) and COP the third most volatile (10.6%), yet both receive small positive weights, because their covariance
with the rest of the portfolio is low relative to their own volatility, so a small holding adds diversification
rather than risk (the underlying correlations are examined in B1). By contrast, CMCSA has much lower volatility
than COP (6.9% against 10.6%) but receives nothing, because its returns move too closely with the stocks already
held.

**Why some stocks receive zero weight.** BBY, CMCSA and SLB have betas to the portfolio above 1 (1.026, 1.059 and
1.229; Table A3.3). Even at the optimum, each would add more risk at the margin than the stocks already held, so
any positive weight would raise portfolio variance; with short selling ruled out, the best the optimiser can do is
hold none. SLB is the clearest case: high volatility (11.9%) combined with the largest covariance with the
portfolio (15.41 (%)²). The portfolio already has a small amount of energy exposure through COP.

**Is the allocation genuinely conservative?** Relative to the alternatives, yes. Its volatility of 3.54% a month is
28% lower than holding MCD alone (4.94%) and 25% lower than an equal-weighted portfolio (4.71%), and its maximum
drawdown (−12.3%) is about half that of MCD (−23.2%). This lower risk came at little cost in return: the expected
return (1.15%) is only slightly below equal weighting (1.30%), so the Sharpe ratio (0.284) is higher than both
benchmarks and higher than every individual stock except MSFT (0.321). The portfolio is also reasonably
diversified, with an effective number of holdings of 5.1 (Table A3.2). In dollar terms, on John and Mary's
\$1.5 million, the worst month would have cost about \$128,000 and the largest fall about \$185,000.

**The limitation of calling an equity-only portfolio "low risk".** "Low risk" here only means low risk compared
with other combinations of these ten shares. An annual volatility of 12.3% is still far above that of cash or
high-quality bonds, and a fall of \$185,000 would be a significant loss for a retired couple. Several factors
suggest that true risk is higher than these figures show. First, the weights were chosen to minimise variance on
this specific sample, so in-sample volatility is flattering; out-of-sample volatility is usually higher, as tested
in J3. Second, 2015–2024 did not include a prolonged crisis of the 2008 kind, so the historical maximum drawdown may
understate what could happen. Third, A2 showed heavy tails for several stocks, so variance understates the chance
of extreme months, and correlations tend to rise in crises, weakening diversification exactly when it is needed.
Finally, about 70% of the portfolio sits in three companies, so it still carries company- and sector-specific risk
that a broader portfolio would not. For John, this allocation is a sensible conservative way to hold these shares,
but genuine capital preservation would also require holding part of the savings outside equities, which lies
outside the scope of this ten-stock analysis.

# Student 2 – Individual Tasks (B1–B3)
#B1 Dependence and Diversification

```{r b1-correlation}
Cor <- cor(Rm)
kable(round(Cor, 2), caption = "Table B1.1: Correlation matrix of monthly returns (estimation sample)")

upper    <- which(upper.tri(Cor), arr.ind = TRUE)
pair_tab <- data.frame(Stock_1     = tickers[upper[, 1]],
                       Stock_2     = tickers[upper[, 2]],
                       Correlation = Cor[upper])
pair_tab <- pair_tab[order(pair_tab$Correlation), ]

kable(rbind(head(pair_tab, 5), tail(pair_tab, 5)), digits = 3, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "Table B1.2: Five lowest and five highest pairwise correlations")

pair_cors  <- Cor[upper.tri(Cor)]
avg_cor    <- mean(pair_cors)
avg_cor_by <- (colSums(Cor) - 1) / (k - 1)

c(Average_correlation = avg_cor, Negative_pairs = sum(pair_cors < 0),
  Strong_pairs_0.7 = sum(abs(pair_cors) >= 0.7), Weak_pairs_0.3 = sum(abs(pair_cors) < 0.3))
round(sort(avg_cor_by), 3)
```
